Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Summary 2 Object of the game 3 Setup of your game on Board Game Arena 3.1 Game Type 3.2 Game Variants 4 Playing a hand of cards 5 Exchanging of cards 6 Start Space 7 Eating and Skipping 8 Entering the home zone 9 To play or not to play - being blocked 10 Effects of cards 11 Note: in case one player quits the game Summary Tock is a card-and-board game for 2 to 6 players. With 4 or 6 players, it is possible to create two or three teams of 2 players, sitting opposite of each other. The game concept is the same as Ludo, Sorry! or Mensch ärgere Dich nicht: Each player owns 4 pawns, has to bring them out of their start area into the game circle, and then race them into their home zone. The difference is that the players don't roll a die. Instead, standard playing cards (like those used in Bridge or Rummy) are dealt to the players, and they can choose to play one of their cards to move a pawn. Object of the game In single player games (no teams), the winner is the player who is first to get all 4 pawns into their home. In team games, the winner is the team that is first to get the pawns of both players into their corresponding homes. After the first player of a team has brought all of their pawns into their home, both players continue to play with the remaining color. Setup of your game on Board Game Arena Game Type You can choose between three game types. Free-for-all : This is the single player game, everyone fights for themselves, no mercy, no friends, just run and eat every pawn that has the wrong color. 2 vs 2 : When you get 4 players at your table, there will be two teams with two players. Assuming that players A1 and A2 belong to team A, and B1,B2 to team B, then the turn order will be A1, B1, A2, B2. With any other number of players, you will play Free-for-all. 2 vs 2 vs 2 : When you get 6 players at your table, there will be three teams with two players each. The turn order will be A1, B1, C1, A2, B2, C2. When you choose team game (2 vs 2, or 2 vs 2 vs 2) new options appear which enable you to set the teams. Default is random. Note: the team games options are still selectable with the wrong number of players so that not to jam the interface. However, if the option is still on with the wrong number of players, it would be free-for-all by default. Game Variants If you are a new player , it is suggested to start with the base game (no variants) -- then you can skip to the "Playing a hand of cards" section below. Details below. I.e., because it can be frustrating when the game starts and you don't have any card to let you start, there is the "start configuration" variant that allow you to place your first pawn on your start space before the game starts (Fast Start). • Use variants? Yes / No If you choose no, the game is played without any variant. After choosing yes you now have to select which variants you want to add among the options which now appear. All variants are compatible with each other. This two-step system has been chosen in order not to spam the interface to new-commers who should start with basics. All options for variant default on base game, so if you just choose "yes" for the option "Use variants?" and change nothing else before launching, you still have the base game without variants. For each drop-down list, variant options are marked with a * symbol between brackets. Bold = the title above the drop-down list Italics = the option to choose for that variant. • Start configuration : Fast start: one pawn in play You start with a pawn already in play on the starting of your color. The other three pawns are still to be put in play later using an Ace or a King. This pawn is a blocker while it does moves from its field, as if it was freshly put in play. [Rating: 1/10] Sorry! with cards.  Decisions are obvious and there is a huge dollop of luck involved with the outcome.

[Rating: 1/10] Bad. Bad game. I get the idea of seeing your hand of cards ahead of time letting you do some sort of strategic something as opposed to it being entirely roll and move, but it also means you'll have hands where you know you are missing your next 4 turns. 4 turns in a row where you will do nothing and your involvement in the game means nothing. That's awful.

[Rating: 2/10] An uninteresting roll-and-move game lumbered with terrible game-lengthening rules over generations.

[Rating: 2/10] Adding hand management to Ludo/Sorry did make it marginally more interesting, but we had a game that felt like it would never end as players constantly hit each other back to the start and the conclusion of the game really dragged out, so many of the problems still remain despite the addition of a strategy element.

[Rating: 2.5/10] Yes, is better to play with cards than with dice, as there are more control over the results, including the order to play. Still, the game is chuck full of luck, as the draw of cards matters a lot.  Furthermore, many turns can be lost while waiting for an Ace or a King, to place a pawn in play - no fun at all and can ne quite frustrating.  [thing=32346][/thing] isn't broken, nor is totally a luck-fest or take-that land. Still, is vastly a sub-par game, that can last for way too long, and be quite boring and infuriating. It is definitely a pass.

[Rating: 4/10] I have a few great childhood memories with this, and I can enjoy myself a bit playing this now (but not much).

[Rating: 4/10] Rating 4 for the partnership game. Totally bl*ws as an everyone-for-themselves game (rating 2) because of the game stalling.  Most recent play on BGA: I could play 1 pawn on my own for two hands, bringing it home on auto-pilot. Then, the next 5 hands I had to sit out and discard. The other players meanwhile were underway. This sitting out on a crap hand (no K or A) really needs a fix. (Maybe as your turn: show hand, discard, then draw new cards minus one. On next turn, repeat if needed. At least you get another shot at progress instead of merely discarding.)
